planting.note: Sow seed on the soil surface in early spring, since it needs light to germinate, into a lean, sharply drained, alkaline to neutral rock garden or wall-top site in full sun; established plants tolerate poor, dry soil far better than rich or damp ground.

directions: Grow basket-of-gold in gritty, fast-draining, lean to average soil in full sun, choosing a slope, dry wall, or raised bed where winter moisture cannot collect around the woody crown. This spreading, gray-leaved subshrub explodes each early spring into a solid dome of small, bright golden-yellow, four-petaled flowers held in dense clusters just above the foliage, making it a cornerstone of the traditional rock garden color palette alongside purple aubrieta and white rock cress. Shear the plant back by roughly a third immediately after flowering to prevent the mat from splitting open in the center, encourage denser regrowth, and keep the naturally short-lived, semi-woody clumps vigorous for several more seasons. It is highly drought tolerant once established and generally shrugs off heat, but resents heavy, wet, or poorly drained soils, which shorten its lifespan considerably.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Citrina Basket-of-Gold (Pale Lemon-Yellow Rock Garden Alyssum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; propagate this named selection by division or cuttings rather than seed to keep its softer flower color true.

directions: 'Citrina' is a soft, pale sulfur-yellow selection of basket-of-gold, chosen for gardeners who find the species' saturated gold too strident next to pastel spring companions like candytuft or pink creeping phlox. It shares the same mat-forming, gray-green foliage and dense April-to-May bloom of the species, and is grown under identical conditions: sharp drainage, full sun, and lean soil that discourages the floppy, short-lived growth that heavier ground produces. Cut the mounds back hard once flowering finishes to keep the habit tight and to prevent the woody centers from opening up and dying out over a few seasons. Because it is a selected clone, propagate new plants by division of rooted sections or by softwood cuttings taken after bloom rather than by seed, which will not come true.

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery-grown plants in spring in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; the tighter habit of this dwarf selection suits small troughs and wall crevices where the standard species would sprawl too far.

directions: 'Compacta' is a dwarf, tighter-mounding form of basket-of-gold bred for small-scale rock gardens, troughs, and wall crevices where the full-sized species would quickly outgrow its space. It produces the same profusion of bright golden four-petaled flowers over gray-green foliage in early to mid-spring, but stays noticeably lower and denser, needing less aggressive post-bloom shearing to hold its shape. Grow it exactly as you would the species: lean, sharply drained, alkaline to neutral soil and full sun, with excellent winter drainage to prevent crown rot. A light trim after flowering keeps the small mounds from thinning out in their centers as they age.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Siberian Whitlow-Grass (Creeping Mat-Forming Rock Garden Draba)

planting.note: Sow seed in fall or plant divisions in spring into ordinary, well-drained rock garden or border-edge soil in full sun; unlike its tight-cushion relatives, this species tolerates average garden conditions and spreads readily by creeping stems.

directions: Siberian whitlow-grass forms a loose, fast-spreading mat of small hairy leaves on creeping stems, quite unlike the tight, hard cushions of most rock garden Draba species, and is correspondingly one of the easiest members of the genus to grow. In earliest spring it disappears under a haze of small, bright-yellow, four-petaled flowers held just above the foliage on short stems, giving an early splash of color before most other rock garden plants have started growth. It tolerates ordinary, well-drained garden soil rather than demanding the scree or tufa conditions of the alpine cushion Drabas, making it a good choice for path edges, wall tops, or the front of a mixed border as well as the rock garden proper. Because it spreads readily, divide congested patches every few years in spring to keep it within bounds and to renew vigor.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall, or set out small rooted pieces, into a lean, sharply drained scree, trough, or tufa mix in full sun; this extremely slow-growing cushion needs its crown kept dry and elevated on grit through winter to avoid rot.

directions: Moss draba forms one of the hardest, tightest cushions in the rock garden, a dense hummock of minute gray-green rosettes so compact it is often mistaken for a mound of moss or a small saxifrage when out of flower. In spring it produces disproportionately large numbers of tiny, bright-yellow, four-petaled flowers on very short stems that sit almost directly on the cushion surface. Growth is extremely slow, so plant it where it will not be crowded out by more vigorous neighbors, and top-dress regularly with fine grit to keep moisture away from the crown. Like most true cushion alpines it is far more tolerant of cold than of winter wet, and is best grown in a trough, raised scree bed, or tufa block with a sharply drained, gritty, lean mix.

planting.note: Plant rooted pieces or nursery starts in spring at the top of a wall, trough edge, or raised bed in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; trailing stems root readily where they touch soil, making later propagation by division or cuttings straightforward.

directions: Trailing rock jasmine is one of the most garden-tolerant androsace species, producing long, silver-haired trailing stems that cascade attractively over the edge of a wall, trough, or raised bed rather than forming the tight, demanding cushions typical of the genus. In mid-to-late summer, later than most rock jasmines, it produces rounded clusters of small pink flowers with a contrasting green-yellow eye scattered along the trailing growth. It appreciates the same sharp drainage and full sun as its alpine relatives but is noticeably more forgiving of average garden heat and handling, making it a good introduction to the genus for gardeners new to androsace. Trim back straggly growth after flowering to keep the mat tidy and encourage fresh new trailing stems for the following season.

planting.note: Plant offsets or rooted rosettes in spring into a gritty, sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun; the flattened, semi-succulent rosettes resent standing moisture and are best raised slightly on a grit layer.

directions: This Himalayan rock jasmine forms a spreading mat of flattened, semi-succulent rosettes connected by short stolons, giving the foliage a distinctly Sempervivum-like appearance that gives the species its name. In late spring, each mature rosette sends up a short cluster of pink flowers with a small yellow eye, held just above the foliage in a neat, dense display. It needs the sharp drainage and full sun typical of Himalayan cushion alpines, growing best in a scree bed, trough, or raised bed with a gritty, lean mix, and resents any prolonged winter wet around the crown. Established mats spread slowly by rosette offsets, which can be detached and rooted separately to increase or renew a planting.

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in fall or early spring at a slight angle in an extremely well-drained, gritty crevice, trough, or raised scree bed in full sun; in climates with wet summers, overhead protection from a pane of glass or an alpine house greatly improves survival.

directions: Tweedy's lewisia is generally regarded as the showiest but most demanding member of the genus, producing large, satiny, apricot-to-peach-pink flowers, sometimes two to three inches across, over evergreen rosettes of thick, paddle-shaped leaves. Native to dry, rocky slopes on the east side of the Cascades in Washington and adjacent British Columbia, it needs the same perfect drainage as Lewisia cotyledon but is even less tolerant of summer moisture around its crown, and gardeners in humid or wet-summer regions often grow it under an alpine-house pane of glass or in a steeply tilted crevice where rain runs off immediately. Plant at an angle rather than flat so water cannot pool against the rosette, and keep the root run lean and gritty with minimal organic matter. Established plants resent disturbance, so choose a permanent site and avoid transplanting once settled in.

common_name: Sunset Strain Lewisia (Vivid Multicolor Siskiyou Lewisia)

planting.note: Plant in spring at a slight angle into fast-draining, gritty, lean soil in full sun, in a rock crevice, trough, or raised bed; this seed strain gives a wide, unpredictable mix of colors, so grow several plants together for the full range.

directions: 'Sunset Strain' is a widely grown seed strain of Siskiyou lewisia selected for an especially vivid and varied color range, producing sprays of flowers in shades of orange, salmon, hot pink, yellow, and magenta, frequently with contrasting darker veining, over evergreen rosettes of fleshy leaves. Grow it exactly as the species: tilted in a rock crevice, trough, or raised scree bed with extremely sharp drainage, since the thick taproot and crown rot quickly if water is allowed to stand around them. Because it is raised from seed rather than a single clone, expect meaningful variation in flower color and pattern from plant to plant, which is part of the strain's appeal for a mixed rock garden planting. Reduce watering sharply once the spring bloom finishes and the plant moves into its summer semi-dormancy.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter under bright light for planting out after the danger of hard frost, into fast-draining, gritty soil in full sun; this compact F1 strain often flowers in its first year when started early.

directions: 'Elise' is a compact, densely flowering F1 seed strain of Siskiyou lewisia, bred for a tighter rosette habit and abundant semi-double blooms in a mixed palette of pink, orange, and yellow shades compared with the more open growth of the species. Its smaller stature makes it well suited to shallow troughs and small crevice plantings where a full-sized Lewisia cotyledon would eventually crowd its neighbors. Culture is identical to the species: extremely sharp drainage, full sun, and a lean, gritty mix, with the crown kept clear of standing water year-round to prevent rot. Started indoors in late winter, seedlings often reach flowering size and bloom the same year, unlike many rock garden perennials that need a full season to establish first.
